subject: ChiShona
curriculum: Zimbabwe Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (MoPSE) - Indigenous Languages Primary Syllabus
syllabus_source: Indigenous Languages Primary (Infant to Junior) Teacher's Guide, 2015-2022 - official MoPSE/ZIMSEC document, verified and fetched directly
confidence_flag: The SKILLS STRUCTURE and GRADE-BY-GRADE TOPIC PROGRESSION (sections marked 'strand_structure') are directly sourced from the official national syllabus document and are verified/reliable. ChiShona is taught using this same national structure as isiNdebele, in the learner's own language. The actual VOCABULARY/PHRASE content (sections marked 'strand_content') is standard, well-established ChiShona language content grounded in general linguistic knowledge of the language - it was NOT extracted from the official textbook's specific word lists (those weren't accessible), so treat vocabulary choices as representative/standard rather than verbatim-official. Core grammar and vocabulary facts are accurate.

chunks.topic: Structure of the Indigenous Languages Syllabus
chunks.content: ChiShona is taught under the national Indigenous Languages syllabus, which covers ECD A through Grade 7 as a single spiral curriculum: the same four skills (Listening/Observing, Speaking/Signing, Reading, Writing/Brailling) and broadly the same topics are covered at every grade, gaining in breadth and depth as learners progress. At the Infant level (ECD A - Grade 2), the learner's indigenous language (ChiShona in Shona-speaking areas) serves as the medium of instruction across the whole curriculum, not just as a language subject. From Grade 3, it continues as a dedicated subject alongside English. The syllabus is explicitly designed to inculcate the values of Unhu/Ubuntu/Vumunhu and to promote and cherish Zimbabwean identity.

At Junior level, ChiShona is assessed through continuous assessment (30% of the final mark, covering drawing, speaking, written exercises, theory exercises, and research projects on culture and heritage) and summative assessment (70%). Summative assessment has two papers: Paper 1 (40 marks) consists of 40 multiple-choice questions covering register, aspects of culture, comprehension, language usage and language structure; Paper 2 (30 marks) has Section A (composition - candidates choose one from five questions) and Section B (comprehension and summary, 5 marks each).

Listening/Observing topics progress from Grade 3's sounds made by objects/animals/materials, word sounds, rhymes/jingles/riddles, dialogue, news/stories/folktales, instructions and times of day; through Grade 4-5's phonetic sounds, totems, sustained dialogue and stress/intonation work; to Grade 6-7's debates on cross-cutting themes, voice and mood in speech, and messages from different media. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to retell folktales, identify moral lessons from folktales, and demonstrate understanding by answering questions. Common activities include storytelling, retelling stories and news, drama, role play, memory games, and singing songs and rhymes to strengthen listening skills.
learning_activities: Listening to and retelling ChiShona folktales, identifying the moral lesson (dzidziso)
Playing sound and memory games with radios, percussion instruments and ICT tools
Listening to and discussing debates on cross-cutting themes in upper grades

chunks.content: Speaking/Signing topics progress from Grade 3's likes/dislikes, roles of self and family members, counting games, reciting rhymes and folktales; through Grade 4-6's totems, myths and taboos, heritage sites, natural resources, debates on cross-cutting themes, and appropriate registers/requests; to Grade 7's prepared and unprepared speeches, riddles/idioms/proverbs, common myths and legends, and figurative expressions. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to tell stories on emerging and cross-cutting themes, debate, dramatise, recite poems and rhymes, and retell folktales.
learning_activities: Reciting rhymes, jingles and riddles (zvirahwe) in ChiShona
Debating cross-cutting themes using appropriate register
Presenting prepared and unprepared speeches by Grade 7

chunks.content: Reading topics progress from Grade 3's syllable sounds, words and sentences, news/stories/folktales, extensive reading, and simple graphs/maps/tables; through Grade 4-6's meanings of words from context, referencing skills, skimming and scanning, idioms/similes/proverbs/ideophones (zvirungamutauro), and inferences; to Grade 7's modern and ancient ways of communication, and continued work on comprehension, intonation and enunciation. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to read a variety of materials, demonstrate understanding through answering questions, and comment on emerging and cross-cutting issues read.
learning_activities: Reading ChiShona texts for comprehension and identifying idioms and proverbs (tsumo)
Practising skimming and scanning skills on graphs, maps and tables in Shona
Discussing modern and traditional ways of communication in Grade 7

chunks.content: Writing/Brailling topics progress from Grade 3's Nelson's script handwriting, punctuation, comprehension questions, creative writing, spelling and dictation, composition, and idioms/riddles/similes/proverbs; through Grade 4-6's poems and prose, summaries, business and friendly letters, telegrams, emails, blogs, essays with linking paragraphs, and information from graphs/pictures/tables; to Grade 7's continued essays, short stories, folktales, creative work, comprehension, summary, spelling, dictation and punctuation, plus ICT tools in writing throughout. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to write creative works, write in appropriate register, and write with grammatical accuracy, correct spelling and appropriate punctuation.
learning_activities: Practising Nelson's script handwriting in ChiShona from Grade 3
Writing formal and informal letters in ChiShona by Grade 5-6
Composing essays, short stories and folktales with correct spelling and punctuation by Grade 7

chunks.content: Common ChiShona greetings: 'Mhoro' (Hello, informal, singular), 'Mhoroi' (Hello, formal/plural or to an elder), 'Makadii?' (How are you? - formal/plural), 'Wakadii?' (How are you? - informal, singular), 'Ndiripo, makadiiwo?' (I am fine, and how are you?), 'Ndiri kunzwa zvakanaka' (I am feeling well). Time-of-day greetings: 'Mangwanani' (Good morning), 'Masikati' (Good afternoon), 'Manheru' (Good evening). Farewells: 'Chisarai zvakanaka' (Stay well, said by the one leaving) / 'Fambai zvakanaka' (Go well, said by the one staying). 'Ndatenda' or 'Maita basa' means thank you; 'Ndine urombo' means I am sorry.

ChiShona numbers 1-10: potsi/imwe chete (1), piri (2), tatu (3), china (4), shanu (5), tanhatu (6), nomwe (7), sere (8), pfumbamwe (9), gumi (10). Numbers 11-20 are typically formed as 'gumi ne-X' (ten and X): gumi neimwe (11), gumi nembiri (12), gumi netatu (13), continuing to makumi maviri (20, literally 'two tens'). Note that ChiShona numbers agree grammatically with the noun class of the object being counted (concordial agreement), so the exact form of the number word changes depending on what is being counted - e.g. 'vana vaviri' (two children) versus 'mabhuku maviri' (two books).

Common ChiShona family/kinship terms: 'Amai' (mother), 'Baba' (father), 'Mwana' (child), 'Mukoma' (older brother, used by a younger sibling), 'Munin'ina' (younger sibling of the same sex), 'Hanzvadzi' (sibling of the opposite sex), 'Sekuru' (grandfather / maternal uncle - an important culturally significant relative), 'Ambuya' or 'Mbuya' (grandmother), 'Tete' (paternal aunt - also an important culturally significant relative in Shona custom), 'Sahwira' (a close family friend with special ceremonial roles). Shona kinship terms often carry specific cultural roles and responsibilities beyond the direct English translation - for example, 'Sekuru' and 'Tete' have recognised roles in family ceremonies and guidance.

chunks.topic: Days of the Week and Time (Mazuva)
chunks.content: ChiShona days of the week: Muvhuro (Monday), Chipiri (Tuesday), Chitatu (Wednesday), China (Thursday), Chishanu (Friday), Mugovera (Saturday), Svondo (Sunday). Time-related vocabulary: 'Nhasi' (today), 'Mangwana' (tomorrow), 'Nezuro' (yesterday), 'Gore' (year), 'Mwedzi' (month), 'Vhiki' (week, a loanword).

ChiShona, like other Bantu languages, organises nouns into noun classes, each marked by a characteristic prefix, which also determines the agreement pattern for adjectives, verbs and pronouns referring to that noun. Common classes include: Class 1/2 (mu-/va-, mostly people, e.g. 'munhu' person / 'vanhu' people), Class 3/4 (mu-/mi-, mostly plants and objects, e.g. 'muti' tree / 'miti' trees), Class 5/6 (ri-(or zero)/ma-, e.g. 'zino' tooth / 'meno' teeth), Class 7/8 (chi-/zvi-, e.g. 'chinhu' thing / 'zvinhu' things), and Class 9/10 (N-/N-, often animals, e.g. 'imbwa' dog / 'imbwa' dogs, same form but different agreement). Understanding noun class is essential because it drives subject-verb agreement and adjective agreement throughout a ChiShona sentence.

Common ChiShona colour terms: 'Chena' (white), 'Tema' (black), 'Tsvuku' (red), 'Girini' (green, a loanword; also described descriptively), 'Bhuruu' (blue, a loanword). Basic descriptive adjectives: 'Kukura' (big), 'Kudiki'/'kudoko' (small), 'Refu' (long/tall), 'Pfupi' (short), 'Chakanaka' (good/nice), 'Chakaipa' (bad). As with nouns, adjectives take a prefix that agrees with the noun class of the thing being described.

Useful everyday ChiShona phrases: 'Ndinoda mvura' (I want water), 'Ndine nzara' (I am hungry, literally 'I have hunger'), 'Ndiri kuenda kuchikoro' (I am going to school), 'Munonzi ani?' (What is your name? - formal), 'Ndinonzi...' (My name is...), 'Ndapota' (Please), 'Hongu' (Yes), 'Kwete' (No), 'Ndiripo' (I am here/fine), 'Handisi kunzwa' (I don't understand / I can't hear).

Totems (mitupo) are a distinctive feature of Shona culture, functioning as clan identifiers passed down patrilineally, usually associated with an animal or natural object (e.g. Shumba/lion, Moyo/heart, Nzou/elephant, Shava/eland, Soko/monkey). Each totem is typically accompanied by praise names (zvidawo) recited to show respect, especially to elders, and totems play an important role in regulating marriage customs (people sharing the same totem are traditionally considered too closely related to marry) and in identity and respect within Shona society. The syllabus's Speaking/Listening strands reference totems from Grade 4 onward, building in depth through to Grade 7's inclusion of totems and their poems (nhetembo dzemitupo).

Madimikira (idioms) are figurative expressions whose meaning cannot be worked out from the literal meaning of the individual words - they must be learned as fixed expressions. They are one of the four categories of 'zvirungamutauro' (figures of speech) in the ChiShona syllabus, alongside tsumo (proverbs), fananidzo (similes) and nyaudzosingwi/zvidudzirapo (ideophones). When answering an exam question asking learners to explain a dimikira, the correct approach is to give the idiomatic meaning directly (not a literal translation), state it briefly and clearly, and avoid simply repeating the idiom back as the answer.

Kukwenya mhuno nekasiyanwa = kutarisira zvinofadza (to scratch the nose with the little finger = to anticipate/expect something pleasant, e.g. good news). Kutemwa dzinobuda ropa = kuva munhu anenge achiri kuzvinzwa / kuva munhu mudiki (to be struck by things that draw blood = to still be young/immature and yet think highly of oneself). Kuva mudenga rechinomwe = kufarisisa (to be in the seventh sky = to be extremely happy). Kutsika mwedzi = kuita pamuviri (to step on the moon = to become pregnant). Kunyura muzvipfeko = kugarwa nezvipfeko zvaunge wapfeka (to sink/drown in one's clothes = to be wearing clothes that are far too big). Kumwisa mvura = kudadisa/kufadza/kuyemura (to give water to drink = to impress, please, or be admired). Kubatira ura mumaoko = kutya zvikuru (to hold one's intestines in one's hands = to be terrified).

chunks.topic: Additional Idioms Used in Syllabus Exercises
chunks.content: The following idioms appear in official ChiShona teaching exercises as expressions learners are asked to interpret: Kurova gotsi nechitsitsinho, Kubereka tsoka, Kuzvisikira moto muziso, Kurova imbwa wakaviga mupini, Kuseura gotsi, Kufira mafufu segonzo, Kushaya ganda kumeso, and Kufumobata jongwe muromo. These are genuine idioms drawn from real ChiShona teaching material, but their specific glosses were presented as an interpretation exercise for learners rather than given directly in the source, so exact meanings are not confirmed here - treat these as idioms worth practising interpretation of in class, not as verified definitions.

Tsumo (proverbs, called shumo in the Karanga dialect) are traditional, fixed sayings that encode moral lessons, social wisdom, and cultural values, typically passed down orally through generations. Structurally, Shona proverbs are usually bipartite (in two balanced parts) and often use vivid imagery from nature, farming, animals and everyday rural life to convey their message. They are used in everyday speech, in formal address, and in storytelling to reinforce social norms such as patience, humility, community cooperation, and respect for elders.

Regai dzive shiri mazai haana muto = musamhanyire zvinhu zvisati zvasvika paukuru hwazvo (let them remain eggs, eggs have no gravy = do not rush into things before their proper time; often used to caution against marrying too young). Nyimo dzinokura pasi pevhu = kuti uwane budiriro unofanira kushanda nesimba, zvinhu zvakanaka hazviuyi wakagara pasi (beans grow underground = success requires effort, good things do not come easily). Doro harisi chinhu chaungavimba nacho serwendo = kusavimba nezvinhu zvisina kusimba (beer is not something to rely on for a journey = do not depend on frivolous or unreliable things for serious matters). Aive madziva ava mazambuko = vanhu vaimbova vakuru/vane simba zvino vava vanhu zvavo, zvinhu zvaimbova zvakaoma zvava nyore (what used to be deep pools are now shallow crossing points = people or things that used to be great/difficult are now ordinary/simple).

Akuruma nzeve ndewako = uyo anokupa zano rakanaka kana kukuyambira ndiye shamwari/hama yako chaiyo (the one who bites/nips your ear (to warn you) is your true friend = those who correct or advise you have your best interests at heart). Chara chimwe hachitswanyi inda = kubatana kunopa simba, munhu mumwe chete haakwanisi kuita zvinhu zvakawanda ega (one finger alone cannot crush a louse = unity and cooperation achieve what an individual cannot do alone). Kandiro kanoenda kunobva kamwe = zvaunoitira vamwe zvinodzokera kwauri (a small dish that goes out, a similar one comes back = kindness or wrongdoing shown to others tends to be reciprocated). Chawawana idya nehama, mutorwa haaperi kukupa = zvaunowana ugoverane nehama dzako, nokuti mutorwa haagari achikupa (what you find, share with family; a stranger will not always be the one giving to you = value and share with your own family/community).

chunks.topic: What Zvirahwe Are and How They Are Played
chunks.content: Zvirahwe (riddles) are a traditional oral game and teaching tool: one person poses a riddle ('chirahwe') and others try to guess the answer ('mhinduro'). Traditionally, children would form two teams - one team poses riddles, the other tries to solve them; a team that fails keeps being asked until they get it, and the winning team is the one that solves the most. Riddles sharpen children's thinking skills while entertaining them, and often describe an everyday object or natural phenomenon through a vivid, indirect image rather than naming it directly.
learning_activities: Playing zvirahwe in teams, taking turns posing and solving riddles
Matching a riddle to its correct answer from multiple choice options
Creating original riddles about familiar objects using indirect, descriptive imagery

chunks.content: Kakomana kariga ishe padare - Mhinduro: hope (a little boy who disrespects/tells off a chief in public - Answer: sleep, because sleep overcomes even a chief). Gumbeze rababa vangu risingapere kupetwa - Mhinduro: denga (my father's blanket that is never finished being folded - Answer: the sky). Amai ngwee kuchena, mwana ngwee kuchena - Mhinduro: guyo nehuyo (mother very white, child very white - Answer: the grinding stone and its handstone). Ane mhanza ngaarohwe - Mhinduro: ngoma (let the bald-headed one be beaten - Answer: the drum). Baba vangu vanotamba vachifamba vasinganeti - Mhinduro: rwizi (my father plays while walking and never gets tired - Answer: the river). Bhuru rangu raenda kundotiva rikadzoka raonda - Mhinduro: sipo (my bull went to bathe and came back thin - Answer: soap). Chidembo tamba tamba muswe ndakabata - Mhinduro: badza (little polecat, play play, I've caught its tail - Answer: the hoe). Chidyamafuta chisingakori - Mhinduro: banga (the fat-eater that never gets fat - Answer: the knife). Chikomo chinopfungaira mhute - Mhinduro: sadza (the hill/mound that gives off mist/steam - Answer: sadza, the staple cooked meal). Tauro rababa vangu rinogara rakanyorova - Mhinduro: rurimi (my father's speech-organ that is always wet - Answer: the tongue).

chunks.topic: What Fananidzo Are and How They Are Formed
chunks.content: Fananidzo (similes) compare one thing to another well-known thing to vividly describe a quality, using the comparative marker 'se-' (like/as) attached to the thing being compared to. This is one of the five figures of speech ('zvirungamutauro') tested in ChiShona language exams alongside tsumo, madimikira, nyaudzosingwi (ideophones) and fananidzosiri/enzaniso (metaphors). The syllabus explains that language is 'seasoned' ('kurungwa') with these figures of speech the way food is seasoned with salt, to make it richer and more pleasing to hear or read.

Mukomana uyu anokara sebere = this boy is as greedy as a hyena. Anonyima sechapungu chisingadonhedzi minhenga yacho = he/she is as stingy as a vulture that never drops its feathers. Ane hanganwa segunguwo = he/she is as forgetful as a crow. Hanzvadzi yaChipo yakareba somupuranga = Chipo's sibling is as tall as a plank. Vanogara vakachena kunge ngirozi = they stay as clean as angels. Common simile-forming stems used with 'se-' in ChiShona include: sebere (like a hyena - greed), sembavha (like a thief), segunguwo (like a crow - forgetfulness), senyoka (like a snake), sehwiza (like a grasshopper), setsuro (like a hare - speed/cleverness), serutsanga (like dry grass), semvumba (like a buffalo - strength), segonzo (like a mouse), sechura (like a frog).

chunks.topic: What Enzaniso Are and How They Differ from Fananidzo
chunks.content: Fananidzosiri (also called enzaniso in some texts - metaphors) make a direct, implied comparison without using 'se-' (like/as) - instead they typically use a form of 'i-' meaning 'is/is a', stating one thing directly as another for stronger effect than a simile. Where a simile says a boy is 'like' a hyena in greed, a metaphor says the boy simply 'is' a hyena in greed. This makes metaphors a bolder, more forceful figure of speech than similes.

Mukomana uyu ibere pakukara = this boy is a (real) hyena in greed. Sekuru vangu imvumba chaiyo pakurwa = my grandfather is a real buffalo in fighting. Makanaka itsvarakadenga chaiyo = you are truly a rainbow (in beauty). Chamunorwa itsuro chaiyo pakumhanya = what you are competing against is truly a hare at running. Imbongoro chaiyo pakushanda = (he/she) is truly a donkey at working (i.e. very hardworking). In more literary/creative ChiShona writing, metaphors can be more elaborate, for example describing someone's beauty as powerful enough to extinguish a fire ('rwaidzima moto wemakwati') or hair as tender as new grass in a valley in springtime ('ruswiswi rwebani pachirimo').

Nyaudzosingwi (ideophones, sometimes called zvidudzirapo) are vivid, often onomatopoeic descriptive words that convey a sense of manner, sound, colour, smell, action or state in a single expressive word - a distinctive feature of Bantu languages including ChiShona. They are used to add vividness and immediacy to speech and writing, and are one of the five figures of speech tested alongside tsumo, madimikira, fananidzo and enzaniso in ChiShona language exams. Ideophones typically cannot be translated with a single English word - they usually require a descriptive phrase in English to capture their full sense.
